chunks: Abu Ali Al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Al-'Ala' ibn Razin, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from one of the two Imams (peace be upon them), who said:

I asked: 'When a man closes the eyes of the deceased, is ritual bath (ghusl) upon him?' He said: 'If he touches him while he is still warm, then no; but if he touches him after he has cooled, then let him perform ritual bath.' I asked: 'So the one who washes him, does he perform ritual bath?' He said: 'Yes.' I asked: 'Does he wash the deceased, then enshroud him, before he performs ritual bath?' He said: 'He washes the deceased, then washes his hand from the dirt, then puts the shrouds upon him, then he performs ritual bath.' I asked: 'So the one who carries him, is ritual bath upon him?' He said: 'No.' I asked: 'So the one who places him in the grave, is ablution (wudu) upon him?' He said: 'No, except that he may perform ablution from the dust of the grave if he wishes.'

key_terms.الْعَاتِق: The dirt or residue on the hand
key_terms.يُبْرُدُ: To cool down (referring to the body)

ai.seo_question: What are the ritual purity rules for closing the eyes, washing, carrying, and burying the deceased in Shia fiqh?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi details the specific fiqh of ritual purity for those handling the deceased, emphasizing the distinction between major impurity (janabah) requiring ghusl and minor impurity requiring wudu. It highlights the scholarly nuance that while carrying and burying the dead do not mandate full ablution, the washer must perform a specific sequence of washing hands and donning shrouds before ghusl, reflecting the practical jurisprudence of the Imams. The permission to take optional wudu from grave dust underscores the flexibility in maintaining ritual state during burial rites.
